newsitem.title: UK: Head of UK's COI bridges ad agency and govt worlds.
newsitem.headline: Head of UK's COI bridges ad agency and govt worlds.

text.p: Five weeks into his job as chief executive of Britain's Central Office of Information, Tony Douglas said his 30 years in advertising agencies will serve him well in overseeing a government department that is increasingly being run along business lines.

After being ousted as co-chairman of the D'Arcy Masius Benton & Bowles advertising agency in February 1995, Douglas in late August was named chief executive of the COI. He assumed the new post on September 30.

Despite the outward differences between the staid, bureaucratic image of government departments and the flashy world of advertising agencies, Douglas said his ad agency background provides a solid bridge to his new job.

"The government is continuously trying to have these agencies run on commercial lines," Douglas told Reuters in an interview in his plain, government-issue office near Waterloo Station -- an area replete with council housing that is only a few miles yet seemingly a world away from the advertising agency meccas of Soho and Charlotte Street.
"In our case, because we provide a service for other government departments, it means break-even. That's our business target," Douglas said.

"It's not as dissimilar as you might think," he added. "In any business outside, I was running an advertising business, but I had targets to meet every year. ... I'm very well used to the idea of having fixed targets year on year.
Douglas said the same skills that were key to running an ad agency -- motivating and leading people, servicing clients and meeting their needs -- are vital to running the COI.
Because government departments are no longer forced to use the COI for all their advertising, publicity and communications needs, the COI must compete head-to-head with commercial businesses.
"Nobody owes the COI a living," Douglas said. "We have to go pitch and then fight to retain every piece of business that we have, and I suspect that is a shift in culture.

"Perhaps the feeling was that could best be handled by someone used to doing that for many years," he added of why the government tapped him for the job. "That's exactly how it works in an advertising agency. No client stays with you forever."

Advertising is only about half of the COI's business, and the agency is only a procurer of advertising services for its various government clients. The COI is increasingly becoming a procurer of services, rather than a provider, in all its sectors, a move which has shrunk its headcount to about 400 today from 1,700 several years ago.

But Douglas said the COI offers a valuable service to its clients, because it can offer expertise to departments whose advertising needs are too small to require their own full-time staff and because the COI as a media buyer can negotiate good discounts by buying large amounts of advertising time and space.

"Many of the government departments don't have a consistent spend year on year, or indeed throughout the year," Douglas said. "They probably couldn't afford, nor would it be sensible to have their own marketing, media experts full-time on their books."

Douglas admitted that as head of the COI he will be on the receiving end of advertising agency business, involved at times in selecting or de-selecting agenices and advising clients on their advertising campaigns.
But he noted that his mandate is to oversee the COI, not to run just its advertising business.
"I think the thing that we need to concentrate on is producing effective communication for our clients," he said. "The acid test is how we perform in the marketplace."
